nameStory: The "whorled" in whorled loosestrife comes from its distinctive leaf arrangement - sets of four leaves circling the stem at regular intervals, like spokes on a wheel. This whorl pattern is so reliable that the scientific name "quadrifolia" literally means "four leaves," making this one of the easier plants to remember once you spot that telltale arrangement.
description: Whorled loosestrife is a delicate woodland wildflower that stands 1-3 feet tall with a straight, unbranched stem. Its most striking feature is sets of four oval leaves arranged in perfect circles around the stem at regular intervals. In early summer, tiny yellow star-shaped flowers dangle gracefully from thin stalks that emerge from where the leaves meet the stem, creating an elegant tiered display.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Four oval leaves arranged in perfect circles (whorls) around the stem at regular intervals - this is the easiest way to identify this plant even without flowers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers with 5 pointed petals that hang delicately on thin thread-like stalks from the leaf whorls, like little dangling stars

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single straight stem 1-3 feet tall, unbranched and smooth to the touch, with a neat tiered appearance from the regular leaf whorls

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Individual leaves are smooth, oval-shaped, and feel thin and papery when rubbed between your fingers, with no teeth along the edges

habitat: Look for whorled loosestrife in rich, moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially in areas with good leaf litter and partial shade. It thrives in woodland clearings, along shaded stream banks, and in forest edges where the soil stays consistently moist but well-drained.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic whorled leaves already visible, making identification possible even before flowering begins.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in June and July when the delicate yellow flowers dangle from the leaf whorls, creating the plant's most striking display.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small round seed capsules develop, while the leaves may turn yellowish before the plant dies back.
seasonality.winter: Completely dies back to the ground, leaving no above-ground parts visible until the following spring.

funFact: Despite its common name, whorled loosestrife is actually in the primrose family and completely unrelated to the purple loosestrife that clogs wetlands - they just happened to get similar names from early botanists who thought their flowers looked alike!
confusionNotes: The four-leaf whorled arrangement is so distinctive that whorled loosestrife is rarely confused with other plants. The closest look-alike might be Indian cucumber root, but that has broader leaves and completely different white flowers that hang in an umbrella cluster.
contextualKnowledge: The "loosestrife" name comes from an old belief that these plants could calm aggressive animals, literally making them "loose from strife." This woodland species shares only a name with the invasive purple loosestrife - they're in completely different plant families and have totally different growth habits.
compareHints: Among New England's many Lysimachia species, whorled loosestrife is instantly recognizable by its four-leaf whorls - no other loosestrife has this arrangement. Swamp candles grows much taller with a spike of flowers, while creeping Jenny hugs the ground, and fringed loosestrife has pairs of leaves rather than whorls of four.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its loosestrife relatives that tend to be taller with yellow flowers and different leaf arrangements, northern starflower is much shorter with its distinctive white seven-petaled blooms and single whorl of leaves.
Among its loosestrife relatives, swamp candles is unique for its tall, narrow flower spike - most other Lysimachia species have flowers in leaf axils or shorter, broader clusters.
Among New England's loosestrifes, fringed loosestrife is distinctive for its opposite leaves with fringed leaf stems and nodding yellow flowers.
Among its loosestrife relatives in New England, creeping Jenny is unique for its trailing, mat-forming habit - most other Lysimachia species stand upright.
Dotted loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife cousins mainly by those telltale petal spots - no other Lysimachia species has them.
Unlike its loosestrife cousins in the same genus, scarlet pimpernel stays ground-hugging rather than growing upright, and its flowers are much smaller but more intensely colored.
Among the loosestrife family in New England, gooseneck loosestrife is the only one with the distinctive curved white flower spikes.
Unlike its loosestrife relatives that are mostly freshwater plants with showy yellow or white flowers, sea milkwort is the oddball of the family - adapted for salt water and lacking petals entirely.

Yellow loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife relatives by its tall stature and dense yellow flower clusters - most other Lysimachia species in New England are shorter with more scattered flowers.
Among its loosestrife cousins, tufted loosestrife is unique for having flowers that emerge from the sides of the stem rather than at the tips.

Among New England's yellow-flowered loosestrifes, lowland loosestrife is distinguished by its flowers tucked into leaf axils rather than arranged in showy spikes like swamp candles, or whorled around the stem like whorled loosestrife.
Among its loosestrife relatives, lanceleaf loosestrife is distinguished by its alternate (not opposite or whorled) leaf arrangement and narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike its flashy cousin creeping Jenny (regular moneywort), miniature moneywort is truly miniature in every way - much smaller leaves, tinier flowers, and more delicate growth.

Unlike other Lysimachia species in New England that tend to be taller perennials with yellow flowers (like whorled loosestrife or swamp candles), blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny blue-flowered annual that creeps along the ground.
